title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
subtitle: How attackers inject JavaScript into web pages — stored, reflected, and DOM-based XSS with real defences

content.text: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) lets an attacker inject JavaScript into a web page that runs in other users' browsers. Once JavaScript is running in your page's context, the attacker has the same access as your own scripts: cookies, localStorage, DOM content, form values, and the ability to make requests to your API using the victim's session. XSS is consistently in the OWASP Top 10 and is the root cause of many high-profile data breaches.

content.code: STORED XSS (persistent, highest impact): Payload stored in the database, served to all users who visit the page Example: comment field stores Victim: every user who views the comment Fix: sanitize HTML on output, use textContent instead of innerHTML REFLECTED XSS (non-persistent): Payload in the URL, reflected back in the response Example: /search?q= Victim: user who clicks a crafted URL (attacker sends via email/phishing) Fix: encode output, validate input DOM-BASED XSS (client-side only): Payload never hits the server — attacker controls client-side data flows Example: page reads location.hash and writes it to innerHTML // Malicious URL: https://myapp.com/# Victim: user who visits the malicious URL Fix: never write untrusted data to innerHTML/document.write/eval BLIND XSS: Payload fires in an admin panel or logging system, not the public page Example: support ticket input field viewed by an admin Victim: the admin user Fix: treat all stored content as untrusted, regardless of the source

content.text: DOMPurify is the standard library for sanitising HTML. If you allow users to input rich text (bold, links, images) and need to display it as HTML, use DOMPurify: const clean = DOMPurify.sanitize(dirty). It strips all dangerous tags (<script>, event handlers, javascript: URLs) while preserving safe formatting. It's maintained by the security community, used by millions of sites, and updated as new bypass techniques emerge. Don't write your own HTML sanitiser.

questions.question: A page reads: const name = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('name'); div.innerHTML = 'Hello, ' + name; An attacker sends: /page?name=. What type of XSS is this?
options: Stored XSS — the payload is saved to the database
Reflected XSS — the payload comes from the server response
DOM-based XSS — the payload is read from the URL and written to the DOM in client-side JavaScript, never touching the server
Blind XSS — the payload fires in an admin panel
questions.explanation: This is DOM-based XSS. The key clue: the payload comes from location.search (the URL's query string) and is written to innerHTML — entirely in client-side JavaScript. The server never sees the malicious payload; it's processed entirely in the browser. The fix: use textContent instead of innerHTML (which displays text literally, never parses as HTML), or sanitize with DOMPurify before setting innerHTML. DOM-based XSS is harder for WAFs and server-side filtering to catch because the attack is invisible to the server.

faq.q: I use React — am I safe from XSS?
faq.a: Mostly, but not completely. React escapes JSX expressions by default, which prevents the most common XSS patterns. But React doesn't protect you from: dangerouslySetInnerHTML with unclean HTML, href/src attributes set to user-controlled values (javascript: URL injection), string concatenation in template literals used to build HTML, or server-side rendering with unencoded data. The principle is the same: never trust user input, encode output.

examples: The Samy Worm (MySpace, 2005) was the fastest-spreading XSS worm in history. It added Samy Kamkar as a friend and hero to every MySpace user who visited an infected profile. Within 20 hours, over 1 million users were infected. The fix took MySpace offline. The payload was 4 kilobytes of JavaScript in a CSS attribute

Twitter had an XSS vulnerability in 2010 (the 'onMouseOver worm') where hovering over a tweet caused it to retweet itself. Within hours, hundreds of thousands of users had retweeted the infected tweet. XSS vulnerabilities spread virally — one infected page can compromise every visitor
